title: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Agent
shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Agent
summary: A Launch Agent is the per-user half of launchd persistence on macOS. The artifact is a property list file, a plist, placed in /System/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents, or ~/Library/LaunchAgents, and it is loaded by the per-user launchd instance when that user logs in. The keys that matter for detection are Label, which names the task, ProgramArguments, which holds the executable path and its arguments, and RunAtLoad or KeepAlive, which decide whether the job runs at login and whether launchd restarts it when it exits. Because agents are created and run with the logged-in user's rights, they need no administrator password, which is why they appear so often in commodity macOS malware. The detection differentiators against benign agents are subtle: legitimate agents belong to signed applications, live under /Library or the vendor's own support folders, and reference executables inside an application bundle, while malicious ones frequently point at temporary, hidden, or home-directory paths and carry a name borrowed from Apple or a popular vendor. Useful telemetry includes launchctl output, file creation events for plist paths, and process lineage showing launchd as the parent of an unexpected binary.

beginner.definition: A Launch Agent is a small settings file on macOS that tells the system to run a program when you log in. The system reads it from a few fixed folders and starts the program with your own account rights. It is a normal macOS feature that software uses to start helpers automatically.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker can put their program in one of these files, so it runs again every time you log in. No administrator password is needed, because the file belongs to your account. This makes the trick cheap and very common. It also hides well, because real applications use the same folders.
howItWorks: The attacker copies their program into a folder the user account can write to, such as a temporary directory.
They then create a property list file for it in the user's LaunchAgents folder.
Inside that file, the Label key gives the job a name that launchd can track.
The ProgramArguments key tells launchd which executable to start and what to pass to it.
The RunAtLoad or KeepAlive key set to true makes the job run at login and restart when it stops.
When you log in, launchd reads the file and starts the program with your account rights.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where every flatmate has their own alarm clock by the bed. The rule is simple: whatever is listed on your clock goes off when you wake up. Someone quietly swaps your clock for theirs, set to a different tune. Every morning you wake to their alarm and the flat does what that alarm asks, without anyone touching your door.
takeaways: Launch Agents are per-user login items, so they need no administrator rights to install.
Check the plist files in the user's Library folder when you suspect macOS persistence.
Names that copy Apple or a well-known vendor are a common trick, so verify the program path.

objectives: Explain how a Launch Agent differs from a Launch Daemon.
Describe what launchd does with a plist file at user login.
Name the folders where Launch Agent plist files are stored.
Explain the role of the RunAtLoad and KeepAlive keys.
Identify which artefacts to collect from a suspect macOS host.
